startup.name: OpenHack
startup.description: OpenHack is an always on AI security engineer that scans code, runs AI pentests and checks supply chain security, then verifies and prioritizes vulnerabilities to cut false positives. Customers are engineering and security teams. A solo founder in San Francisco, Fall 2026 batch.

yc_acceptance.basis: Blind test: the company is known to have been accepted, so this is a placeholder note and not a real estimate. The prior for a random applicant is about 1 percent (references/yc_acceptance.md), and this team would sit near the middle, with a solo founder as a small negative within that range.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: Not applicable in this test because the company was accepted. If YC had said no, the likely reasons would be a solo founder, a very crowded AI security space where many Winter and Summer 2024 to 2026 companies pitch the same thing, and no clear edge over XBOW or well funded scanners.

ladder.why_it_fails: The probable stop is that a solo founder cannot show customers or benchmark wins fast enough while better known AI pentesting companies raise. XBOW publicly topped HackerOne and raised $75M in 2025, which makes investors ask what a new entrant has that it does not, and CodeAnt and Escape have already taken seed money. Without paid pilots, a round above $500K within a year is at risk.

anchors.adjustment_reason: At the anchor, between the 2022-2025 and 2018-2022 B2B values. Crowding and takeover risk offset hot demand.

bands.rationale: Lower end of the 2022+ Series A range.
Median 2022+ B2B Series A of about $15M.
Upside if growth is rapid and the category leaders set high prices.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series A fails when revenue per customer is low, accuracy claims are hard to prove and large security vendors bundle similar features. Escape (W23) and CodeAnt (W24) reached seed or A but many peers, such as winfunc and ZeroPath, show no round in the data. A solo founder also struggles to hire and sell to enterprises at the pace investors expect.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series B fails if the product competes on price and false positive rate and a platform such as a large code security vendor adds the same features. The market has already seen XBOW raise more than $100M, so a second tier player must show clear differentiation to reach B.

anchors.adjustment_reason: Below the anchor, since a crowded category leaves one or two winners.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series C fails if the category consolidates around one or two leaders and this company is acquired by a larger security platform. DeepSource (W20) was acquired and Patchwork Security (W16) shut down, which shows both small endings.

outcomes.why_it_fails: A solo founder in a crowded and fast moving category is most likely to be outrun by better funded rivals or absorbed by an existing security platform. Patchwork Security shut down and DeepSource sold below $1B, matching the likely ends.

brand.rationale: The name is descriptive and easy to remember, but generic in a crowded field and may suggest offensive hacking rather than a defender. The effect on success is small.

narrative.headline: A hot category with strong leaders makes a solo founder's seed likely but later rounds uncertain.
narrative.general_summary: OpenHack is a solo founder AI security engineer product in the hottest corner of 2026 security investing. Demand is real, since XBOW raised large rounds, and B2B seed rates are near 59% within the cohort, so a seed above $500K is more likely than not. The same heat means many peers, including Escape, CodeAnt, ZeroPath and winfunc, pitch similar tools, and only a few reached Series A in the data. Large vendors can bundle scanning, and a solo founder must show findings and pilots quickly. Later rounds are possible if a wedge emerges, and a pivot to a narrower product is a plausible upside path.

assumptions: Blind test using only the batch start description.
Security tag cohort is too small (n=4), so the B2B cohort is the anchor.
Seed means a round above $500K within about 12 months.
